group.title: Subtle emotions
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Annoyance mixed with embarrassment because something has gone wrong or made you look foolish.
examples: Much to his {chagrin}, the rival he had mocked won the prize.
wrong: She felt pure chagrin when everything went exactly as she had hoped.

words.meaning: A brief feeling of irritation, often because your pride has been hurt.
examples: He left the meeting in a fit of {pique} after his idea was ignored.
wrong: In a fit of pique, she thanked everyone warmly and stayed calm.

words.meaning: Pleasure felt at another person’s bad luck or failure.
examples: There was a hint of {schadenfreude} in his smile when his rival tripped on stage.
wrong: Out of schadenfreude, she wept when her enemy failed.

words.meaning: Without hope and in very low spirits.
examples: After the third rejection letter, she grew {despondent} about finding work.
wrong: He was despondent and could not stop smiling about his future.

words.meaning: A feeling of doubt or worry about whether something is right or will work.
examples: I signed the contract, but I had serious {misgivings} about the deadline.
wrong: My misgivings about the plan made me completely sure it would work.

words.meaning: A feeling of guilt that stops you doing wrong or follows a wrong act.
examples: He took the last slice without the slightest {compunction}.
wrong: She felt deep compunction about the kind gift she had given.

words.meaning: Sincere sorrow for something wrong you have done.
examples: His {contrition} seemed genuine as he apologized to every guest.
wrong: Full of contrition, he boasted about the harm he had done.

words.meaning: A sudden, sharp feeling of a painful emotion.
examples: She felt a {pang} of jealousy when she saw them together.
wrong: A pang of guilt lasted calmly for many peaceful years.

words.meaning: A strong, often sad desire for something you do not have.
examples: Living abroad, he felt a deep {yearning} for his mother’s cooking.
wrong: Her yearning for the sea meant she never wanted to see it.

words.meaning: Pleasant and sad at the same time.
examples: Graduation was {bittersweet}: proud of the past, sorry to leave friends.
wrong: The day was bittersweet, purely joyful with no sadness at all.

words.meaning: A feeling of worry or unease that is quiet but persistent.
examples: The rumors of job cuts caused growing {disquiet} among the staff.
wrong: The good news filled the office with disquiet and relief.

words.meaning: A weary, dissatisfied feeling caused by having nothing interesting to do.
examples: Long summer afternoons filled the teenagers with {ennui}.
wrong: The thrilling adventure filled her with ennui from start to finish.

words.meaning: A pleasant tiredness or lack of energy, often in warm weather.
examples: The heat of the afternoon brought a sweet {languor} over the town.
wrong: Full of languor, he sprinted around the track ten times.

words.meaning: Having no energy or interest in anything.
examples: The illness left him pale and {listless} for weeks.
wrong: She was listless and eagerly threw herself into every task.

words.meaning: Gloomy, silent and bad-tempered.
examples: After losing the match, he sat {morose} in a corner all evening.
wrong: He was morose, laughing and chatting cheerfully with everyone.

words.meaning: Childishly sulky and bad-tempered when you do not get your way.
examples: The star gave a {petulant} reply when asked to wait.
wrong: She stayed petulant and gracious when her request was refused.

words.meaning: Complaining in an irritable, whining way.
examples: The old man’s {querulous} voice rose from the back seat again.
wrong: Her querulous tone showed how content and uncomplaining she was.

words.meaning: To feel offended by something someone says or does.
examples: She {took umbrage} at the suggestion that she had been careless.
wrong: He took umbrage at the compliment and thanked her warmly.

words.meaning: A strong, lasting feeling of hostility between people or groups.
examples: The {enmity} between the two families lasted for generations.
wrong: Their enmity was so strong that they became best friends.

words.meaning: A feeling of intense joy or delight.
examples: The audience listened in {rapture} as she sang.
wrong: He listened in rapture, bored and checking his watch.

words.meaning: Extremely embarrassed and ashamed.
examples: I was {mortified} when I called my teacher by the wrong name.
wrong: She felt mortified, proud and at ease after her mistake.

words.meaning: Embarrassed and a little ashamed, especially after being corrected.
examples: The boy looked {abashed} when his mother found the broken vase.
wrong: He looked abashed, bold and completely unbothered by the scolding.

words.meaning: Slightly embarrassed because you have done something silly.
examples: He gave a {sheepish} grin when he realized he had the wrong date.
wrong: She gave a sheepish smile, proud of her brilliant success.

words.meaning: So unhappy that nothing can comfort you.
examples: The {disconsolate} fans stood in the rain long after the loss.
wrong: She was disconsolate, quickly cheered by a single kind word.

words.meaning: A sudden brief thrill of excitement or fear.
examples: A {frisson} of excitement ran through the crowd as the lights dimmed.
wrong: The dull lecture sent a frisson of total boredom through me.

words.meaning: The state of being annoyed or troubled.
examples: To his {vexation}, the train was delayed yet again.
wrong: To her vexation, everything ran smoothly and on time.

words.meaning: Shock and worry caused by something unexpected.
examples: The sudden closure of the factory caused {consternation} in the town.
wrong: The good news was met with calm consternation and cheers.

words.meaning: Annoyed and dissatisfied, especially about how you have been treated.
examples: {Disgruntled} passengers queued at the desk to complain.
wrong: The disgruntled staff were delighted with their new pay.

words.meaning: Cheerful, full of energy and enthusiasm.
examples: The {ebullient} host greeted every guest with a joke.
wrong: She was ebullient, quiet and gloomy all evening.

words.meaning: Feeling or showing great happiness, especially after a success.
examples: {Jubilant} supporters poured onto the field after the final whistle.
wrong: The jubilant crowd wept bitterly over the defeat.

words.meaning: Sad and sentimental in a foolish or tearful way.
examples: After midnight the party turned {maudlin}, with old songs and tears.
wrong: The maudlin speech was brisk, dry and free of feeling.

words.meaning: Tending to cry easily, or causing tears.
examples: The film’s {lachrymose} ending left the audience reaching for tissues.
wrong: The lachrymose comedy had everyone laughing without a single tear.

words.meaning: Expressing sorrow; looking or sounding mournful.
examples: The puppy gazed up with {doleful} eyes as we left.
wrong: His doleful expression showed how cheerful he felt.

words.meaning: To keep causing bitterness or irritation over a long time.
examples: The unfair decision still {rankles} with him years later.
wrong: The kind remark rankled, so she forgot it at once.

words.meaning: To show or feel great happiness, especially at a triumph.
examples: The team {exulted} in their unexpected victory.
wrong: They exulted in their crushing defeat, heads bowed.

words.meaning: Great happiness and excitement.
examples: There was {elation} in the lab when the experiment finally worked.
wrong: Her elation at the bad news brought her to despair.

words.meaning: A state of mental or physical inactivity and dullness.
examples: A heavy meal left the whole family in a state of {torpor}.
wrong: In his torpor, he leapt up and ran around the garden.

words.meaning: A strong feeling that something bad is going to happen.
examples: She opened the letter with a sense of {foreboding}.
wrong: Full of foreboding, he was sure only good things lay ahead.

words.meaning: The feeling of no longer believing in or admiring something.
examples: His {disenchantment} with politics began after the scandal.
wrong: Her disenchantment with the job made her love it more than ever.

words.meaning: Deeply sad and lonely after a loss; completely lacking something.
examples: She felt utterly {bereft} after her closest friend moved away.
wrong: He was bereft of ideas, so his notebook overflowed with them.
